summary: Discusses aggregating Diffserv service classes inside high-capacity network cores, where some segments may offer only one forwarding treatment for several classes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In a busy highway core, fewer lanes are made for many kinds of vehicles. This explains how to merge several traffic types into one lane.

subtitle: Guidelines for merging Diffserv classes in network cores with limited treatment levels

tldr.problem: High-capacity network cores often have fewer forwarding treatment levels available than the number of Diffserv service classes they must support, requiring a way to merge similar classes without losing end-to-end performance guarantees.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5127 provides guidelines for aggregating multiple Diffserv service classes into four treatment aggregates based on performance requirements: Network Control, Real-Time, Assured Elastic, and Elastic.
tldr.outcome: Networks can simplify core operations by grouping classes with similar characteristics while maintaining per-class treatment at domain boundaries, enabling efficient scaling in high-capacity backbones.

facts.label: Service classes in Real-Time aggregate
facts.value: Telephony, Signaling, Multimedia Conferencing, Real-time Interactive, Broadcast Video

today: RFC 5127 remains an Informational standard and has not been superseded. It is widely used by network operators designing Diffserv domains and MPLS-based backbones to balance simplicity in core routers with the need to preserve end-to-end service quality.

sections.title: Why Service Class Aggregation
sections.content:
High-capacity network backbones are engineered with enough redundancy and capacity to support multiple Service Level Agreements (SLAs) simultaneously. However, real-world networks still face challenges: brief congestion spikes affect real-time applications, while denial-of-service attacks and network disruptions can threaten routing stability.

Diffserv service classes let networks mark packets to indicate their performance needs: delay tolerance, jitter sensitivity, and acceptable loss rates. RFC 4594 defines these classes for applications ranging from voice calls to file transfers. But in a network's core, a single forwarding treatment often suffices for multiple classes. This RFC shows how to safely merge classes without losing the per-hop quality each one needs.
sections.plainLanguage: When a postcard enters the main post office, it might lose its special handling. This explains which postcards can be lumped together without breaking their promises.

sections.title: Service Classes and Treatment Aggregates
sections.content:
A Diffserv service class is a set of traffic with the same performance requirements, identified by a code in the IP header called a DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point). For example, voice (Telephony) needs very low delay and jitter, while file downloads (Standard Data) accept any speed.

A treatment aggregate is a single forwarding queue or scheduling class at a router. When a network has five service classes but only three available queue types, it must merge classes. The RFC's key requirements are: aggregation must preserve the strictest requirements of its member classes, classes must have similar characteristics, and the original DSCP markings should remain unchanged so downstream domains can re-separate them if needed.

For example, voice and video both need very low jitter, so they can share a real-time queue. But file transfers and bulk downloads have different delay tolerance, so they need separate queues or careful management within a shared one.
sections.plainLanguage: Service classes are groups of mail with similar needs (fragile vs. standard). A treatment aggregate is a bin: you can put similar items in one bin, but the bin must be good enough for the most delicate item in it.

sections.title: The Four Treatment Aggregates
sections.content:
RFC 5127 recommends mapping all Diffserv service classes into four aggregates, each with a different forwarding treatment:

Network Control: Protects routing traffic and network management frames. Must have very low loss and deep queues to survive denial-of-service attacks. Uses the Class Selector (CS) PHB with DSCP marking CS6.

Real-Time: Aggregates voice (Telephony), signaling, video conferencing, real-time interactive applications, and broadcast video. All require very low delay and jitter. Requires per-class admission control at the network edge to guarantee that the total traffic entering does not exceed available resources. Uses the Expedited Forwarding (EF) PHB and related markings (EF, CS5, AF41–43, CS3–4).

Assured Elastic: Groups elastic applications that have negotiated a committed rate: multimedia streaming, low-latency data, and operations/administration/management traffic. Traffic can exceed the committed rate but at higher loss risk. Uses the Assured Forwarding (AF) PHB with multiple drop priorities: AFn1 has lowest loss probability, AFn3 highest.

Elastic: Standard internet traffic with no specific SLA. Includes both normal data and low-priority data. Has no guaranteed treatment; is dropped first during congestion. Uses the Default PHB (CS0).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of four mail categories: emergency (network control), phone calls (real-time), insured packages (assured elastic), and regular mail (elastic). Each gets a different shelf in the post office with different handling rules.

sections.title: Forwarding Behavior and Queue Management
sections.content:
Each treatment aggregate must implement specific queue management and drop behavior. The Network Control and Real-Time aggregates aim for minimal packet loss: real-time traffic must not be dropped if admission control works correctly. The Assured Elastic aggregate uses Active Queue Management (AQM) or Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to drop or mark the highest-drop-precedence traffic (AFn3) before AFn2, and AFn2 before AFn1. This preserves committed traffic.

When using Random Early Detection (RED) as the AQM algorithm, the RFC specifies queue thresholds: each drop level (AFn1, AFn2, AFn3) has a minimum and maximum queue depth. This ensures that excess traffic is shed in the right order: bulk, then elastic, then assured, allowing real-time and control traffic to survive.

Domains may employ additional policing and admission control on individual service classes before aggregation, and again on the sum of traffic across the entire aggregate. This two-level control prevents any single class or the aggregate as a whole from exceeding its allocated resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Each type of mail gets treated by different rules. Fragile items rarely get dropped, insured packages get checked before dropping, and junk mail gets dropped first if the bin fills up.

sections.title: Deployment and Inter-Provider Relationships
sections.content:
When networks interconnect at provider boundaries, RFC 5127 recommends negotiating based on the original Diffserv service classes, not the core's internal treatment aggregates. This allows each provider to enforce admission control per class and independently decide how many treatment aggregates to use internally.

The RFC's appendix shows how to implement treatment aggregates using MPLS, a common tunneling technology in backbones. MPLS E-LSP (Explicit Path) tunnels can carry multiple service classes by using the MPLS EXP field (3 bits) to indicate both the treatment aggregate and drop precedence. For example, EXP value 100 signals real-time traffic, while 010 and 011 indicate different drop priorities within assured elastic. This allows MPLS domains to implement the same four-level aggregation while preserving the original DSCP for non-MPLS segments.

The RFC emphasizes that domains retain control: they may support fewer or more aggregates than the four recommended, and business relationships often drive these choices. The key constraint is that whatever aggregation a domain performs should not destroy the ability of downstream domains to identify and re-separate the original service classes.
sections.plainLanguage: When mail crosses a postal border, the central post office should still recognize what country or priority each piece came from, even if the local core uses different internal bins.
